newsitem.title: RWANDA: Burundi's Buyoya to attend summits as war rages.
newsitem.headline: Burundi's Buyoya to attend summits as war rages.

text.p: Breaking his diplomatic isolation, Burundi's military leader Pierre Buyoya flew out of his battle-torn central African state on Sunday to attend two African summits.

Buyoya's trip, his first abroad since he seized power in a coup in July, coincided with a flare-up in Burundi's civil war, with Hutu rebels reporting attacks on army positions in five regions of the country.

Presidential spokesman Jean-Luc Ndizeye told Reuters that Buyoya, whose government was punished with regional economic and transport sanctions after his July 25 coup, left to attend an African summit in Congo on Monday.
He would later visit Burkina Faso in West Africa for a Franco-African summit on Wednesday.

"The (Congo) summit will discuss events in eastern Zaire and in Burundi," Ndizeye said in a telephone interview. He added Angola, Cameroon, Congo, the Central African Republic, Gabon and Zaire would be attending.
Zairean rebels backed by Rwanda's English-speaking Tutsi-dominated army have seized control of much of eastern Zaire and have vowed to take their military campaign to the capital Kinshasa.
On Wednesday, Buyoya will take part in a Franco-African summit despite sanctions imposed on his country after the July coup by Burundi's neighbours -- Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Zambia.
French President Jacques Chirac will also attend the summit of France's African allies which is certain to be dominated by events in Zaire and Burundi.
Buyoya's attendance at the two meetings marks a breakthrough in his efforts to end isolation imposed on him by regional leaders led by Tanzania.

France, worried about the deteriorating situation in Zaire, fears its influence in the rest of Francophone Africa will wane dramatically if it fails to help ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko recover his control over the country.
The three-year-old Burundi civil war which has already killed about 150,000 people is getting worse, aid officials and diplomats said.

Up to 110,000 Burundian Hutus fled fighting between Hutu rebels and the army in south and central provinces in November for camps around Kigoma, in western Tanzania, according to figures provided by the U.N. refugee agency.

But the statistics were disputed by other agencies which said only around 45,000 had fled the fighting between Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels belonging to the Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD).
A Nairobi-based FDD spokesman said on Sunday FDD forces were engaging army positions in five regions of Burundi.

"Thousands of Burundians have left for Tanzania because there has been major combat in Ruyigi (province) in the last two weeks," Annick Hamel, country representative for MSF-France (Doctors Without Borders) said.

The Hutu rebels have been fighting their way across Burundi towards Tanzania since being ejected in October from bases in refugee camps north of the east Zairean town of Uvira now controlled by Rwandan-backed Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels.

Buyoya's army has lately scored a series of victories against the FDD, but Burundi's relations with Tanzania have been damaged by an apparent willingness by Tanzania to harbour the Hutu rebels, diplomats say.
